prompt:
Fix a prime $p$ and let $G$ be a finite group with the property that every nonidentity $p$-subgroup of $G$ is contained in a unique Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$. Suppose $N\trianglelefteq G$ and $|N|$ is divisible by $p$.

(i) If $P$ and $Q$ are Sylow $p$-subgroups of $G$, show that $Q=P^n$ for some element $n\in N$.

(ii) Prove that $G/N$ has a unique Sylow $p$-subgroup.
answer: (i) $P\cap N,\,Q\cap N\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(N)$, so $Q\cap N=(P\cap N)^n$ with $n\in N$; the nonidentity $p$-group $Q\cap N$ lies in both $Q$ and $P^n$, so $Q=P^n$. (ii) Sylow subgroups of $G/N$ are images $PN/N$, and $P^nN/N=PN/N$.

solutions.title: Sylow in the normal subgroup
solutions.body:
**(i)** Since $N\trianglelefteq G$, $P\cap N$ and $Q\cap N$ are Sylow $p$-subgroups of $N$. By Sylow's theorem in $N$, $Q\cap N=(P\cap N)^n$ for some $n\in N$. Because $p$ divides $|N|$, $Q\cap N\neq1$. Now $Q\supseteq Q\cap N$ and $P^n\supseteq(P\cap N)^n=Q\cap N$, and $P^n$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$. By uniqueness of the Sylow $p$-subgroup containing $Q\cap N$, $Q=P^n$.

**(ii)** Let $\bar{\ }\colon G\to G/N$. Every Sylow $p$-subgroup of $\bar G$ is the image $\bar P$ of some $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$. Given two, $\bar P$ and $\bar Q$, (i) gives $Q=P^n$ with $n\in N$, so $\bar Q=\bar P^{\bar n}=\bar P$ since $\bar n=1$. So $G/N$ has a unique Sylow $p$-subgroup. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative domain and write $(a)$ for the principal ideal generated by $a\in R$. Recall that an element of $R$ is said to be irreducible if it is nonzero, not a unit, and has no proper factorization.

(i) Show that $(a)\subseteq(b)$ if and only if $b\mid a$, and that $(a)=(b)$ if and only if $b=au$ for some unit $u\in R$.

(ii) If $R$ is a UFD (unique factorization domain), prove that the set of principal ideals of $R$ satisfies the maximal condition.

(iii) If the set of principal ideals of $R$ satisfies the maximal condition, show that every nonzero, nonunit element of $R$ can be written as a finite product of irreducible elements.
answer: (i) $(a)\subseteq(b)\iff a\in(b)$; mutual divisibility plus cancellation gives a unit. (ii) Choose $(a)$ in the family with the fewest prime factors; a strictly larger $(b)$ would have $b$ a proper divisor with fewer prime factors. (iii) A maximal counterexample $(a)$ factors as $bc$ with $(b),(c)\supsetneq(a)$, which are products of irreducibles.

solutions.title: Counting prime factors
solutions.body:

prompt:
Let $p$ be a prime, let $F\subseteq K$ be fields of characteristic $0$, and assume that $F$ contains a primitive $p$th root of unity. Fix $a\in K$.

(i) Prove that there exists a field $E\supseteq K$ such that $E$ contains a $p$th root of $a$ and $|E:K|=1$ or $p$.

(ii) Now assume that $K$ is a finite degree Galois extension of $F$. Show that there exists a field $E\supseteq K$ such that $E$ contains a $p$th root of $a$, $E$ is Galois over $F$, and $|E:K|$ is a power of $p$.
answer: (i) Let $E$ be the splitting field of $x^p-a$ over $K$; any one root generates it (roots differ by $p$th roots of unity in $F$), so all irreducible factors have degree $|E:K|$, which divides $p$. (ii) Adjoin to $K$ the roots of $\prod_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)}(x^p-\sigma(a))\in F[x]$ one factor at a time; $E$ is a splitting field over $F$, and each step has degree $1$ or $p$ by (i).

solutions.title: Kummer-type towers
solutions.body:
Work in a fixed algebraic closure of $K$; let $\zeta\in F$ be a primitive $p$th root of unity.

**(i)** Let $f=x^p-a$ and let $E$ be its splitting field over $K$. If $a=0$, $E=K$. Otherwise, if $\beta$ is any root, the roots of $f$ are $\zeta^i\beta$ ($0\le i<p$), so $K[\beta]=E$. Factor $f=g_1\cdots g_r$ into irreducibles in $K[x]$, and let $\beta_j$ be a root of $g_j$. Then $\deg g_j=|K[\beta_j]:K|=|E:K|$ for every $j$, so $p=\deg f=r\,|E:K|$. As $p$ is prime, $|E:K|\in\{1,p\}$. Clearly $E$ contains a $p$th root of $a$.

**(ii)** Let $K$ be the splitting field over $F$ of some $g\in F[x]$, and let $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)=\{\sigma_1=1,\sigma_2,\dots,\sigma_n\}$. Put $h(x)=\prod_{i=1}^n(x^p-\sigma_i(a))$. Its coefficients are fixed by $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ (which permutes the factors), so $h\in F[x]$. Let $E$ be the splitting field of $gh$ over $F$; it contains $K$ and a $p$th root of $a$, and $E/F$ is Galois (a splitting field in characteristic $0$).

For $0\le j\le n$ let $E_j$ be the field generated over $K$ by the roots of $\prod_{i\le j}(x^p-\sigma_i(a))$, so $K=E_0\subseteq E_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq E_n=E$. $E_j$ is the splitting field of $x^p-\sigma_j(a)$ over $E_{j-1}$, and $F\subseteq E_{j-1}$ contains $\zeta$, so by (i) $|E_j:E_{j-1}|\in\{1,p\}$. Therefore $|E:K|=\prod_j|E_j:E_{j-1}|$ is a power of $p$. ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space over a field of characteristic $0$. Suppose $T\colon V\to V$ is a linear operator such that the trace $\mathrm{tr}\,T^k=0$ for all integers $k\ge1$.

(i) Show that the constant term of the characteristic polynomial of $T$ is zero, and deduce that $T(V)\neq V$.

(ii) Let $S$ denote the restriction of $T$ to the subspace $T(V)$, so that $S$ is a linear operator on $T(V)$. Prove that $\mathrm{tr}\,S^k=0$ for all integers $k\ge1$.

(iii) Show that $T$ is nilpotent.
answer: (i) Take the trace of Cayley–Hamilton $T^n+a_1T^{n-1}+\cdots+a_nI=0$: $na_n=0$, so $a_n=0$, $\det T=0$. (ii) In a basis extending one of $T(V)$, $T=\begin{pmatrix}A&*\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $\mathrm{tr}\,S^k=\mathrm{tr}\,A^k=\mathrm{tr}\,T^k$. (iii) Induction on $\dim V$: $S$ is nilpotent, so $T^{j+1}=S^jT=0$.

solutions.title: Cayley–Hamilton and induction
solutions.body:
Let $n=\dim V$.

**(i)** Let $\chi(x)=x^n+a_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{n-1}x+a_n$ be the characteristic polynomial. By Cayley–Hamilton, $0=T^n+a_1T^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{n-1}T+a_nI$. Taking traces (trace is linear) and using $\mathrm{tr}\,T^k=0$ for $k\ge1$, we get $0=a_n\,\mathrm{tr}\,I=na_n$. In characteristic $0$, $n\neq0$ (for $n\ge1$), so $a_n=0$. Since $\det T=\pm a_n=0$, $T$ is singular, hence not surjective: $T(V)\ne V$.

**(ii)** $T(T(V))\subseteq T(V)$, so $S$ is well defined. Choose a basis of $T(V)$ and extend it to a basis of $V$. Since $T$ maps $V$ into $T(V)$, its matrix (columns = images) is $B=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, where $A$ is the matrix of $S$. Then $B^k=\begin{pmatrix}A^k&A^{k-1}C\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $\mathrm{tr}\,S^k=\mathrm{tr}\,A^k=\mathrm{tr}\,B^k=\mathrm{tr}\,T^k=0$.

**(iii)** Induct on $n$; for $n=0$ there is nothing to prove. For $n\ge1$, $\dim T(V)<n$ by (i), and $S$ satisfies the hypothesis by (ii), so $S$ is nilpotent by induction: $S^j=0$ for some $j$. Then $T^{j+1}(V)=T^j(T(V))=S^j(T(V))=0$, so $T$ is nilpotent. ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a (not necessarily finite) group and let $\theta\colon G\to G$ be a homomorphism such that $\theta^n(G)=\{1\}$ for some integer $n\ge1$.

(i) If the kernel of $\theta$ is finite, prove that the kernel of $\theta^2$ is finite, and deduce that $G$ is finite.

(ii) If $\theta(G)$ has finite index in $G$, prove that $\theta^2(G)$ has finite index in $G$, and deduce that $G$ is finite.
answer: (i) $\theta$ maps $H=\ker\theta^2$ into $\ker\theta$ with kernel $\ker\theta$, so $|H|\le|\ker\theta|^2$; then induct on $n$ using the induced map on $G/\ker\theta$. (ii) $|\theta(G):\theta^2(G)|\le|G:\theta(G)|$; induct on $n$ using the restriction of $\theta$ to $\theta(G)$.

solutions.title: Induction on the nilpotency exponent
solutions.body:
**(i)** Let $H=\ker\theta^2$. Then $\theta(H)\subseteq\ker\theta$, and the restriction $\theta|_H\colon H\to\ker\theta$ has kernel $H\cap\ker\theta=\ker\theta$. So $|H|=|\theta(H)|\cdot|\ker\theta|\le|\ker\theta|^2<\infty$.

Now show $G$ finite by induction on $n$. If $n=1$, $\theta(G)=1$, so $G=\ker\theta$ is finite. For $n\ge2$, let $K=\ker\theta\trianglelefteq G$. Since $\theta(K)=1\subseteq K$, $\theta$ induces a homomorphism $\varphi\colon G/K\to G/K$, $gK\mapsto\theta(g)K$. Its kernel is $\{gK:\theta(g)\in K\}=\ker\theta^2/K$, which is finite by the above. Also $\varphi^{n-1}(G/K)=\theta^{n-1}(G)K/K=K/K$ is trivial, because $\theta(\theta^{n-1}(G))=\theta^n(G)=1$ gives $\theta^{n-1}(G)\subseteq K$. By induction $G/K$ is finite, and $K$ is finite, so $G$ is finite.

**(ii)** $\theta\colon G\to\theta(G)$ is surjective and maps $\theta(G)$ onto $\theta^2(G)$, so it maps each coset $x\theta(G)$ onto the coset $\theta(x)\theta^2(G)$; hence $|\theta(G):\theta^2(G)|\le|G:\theta(G)|$ and $|G:\theta^2(G)|=|G:\theta(G)|\,|\theta(G):\theta^2(G)|<\infty$.

Induct on $n$. If $n=1$, $\theta(G)=1$ has finite index, so $G$ is finite. For $n\ge2$, let $\varphi=\theta|_{\theta(G)}\colon\theta(G)\to\theta(G)$. Then $\varphi^{n-1}(\theta(G))=\theta^n(G)=1$ and $|\theta(G):\varphi(\theta(G))|=|\theta(G):\theta^2(G)|<\infty$. By induction $\theta(G)$ is finite, and since it has finite index, $G$ is finite. ∎
